title: Metaprogramming and Move Semantics
summary: Why value semantics used to mean expensive deep copies, and how C++11 fixed it: value categories, std::move, forwarding references, reference collapsing and std::forward (with the class's own Forward/Remove_Ref and custom String/vector). Then the Rule of 3/5/0, SSO, SFINAE and C++20 concepts, type traits built by specialisation, RVO/NRVO, compiler-friendly habits, and a first look at unique_ptr/shared_ptr and the control block.

notes.heading: The problem: copies C++ ends up making without good compilers (and before C++11)
L-values and R-values (value categories)
notes.body:
Every expression has a type **and** a value category:

| Category | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **lvalue** | has identity, can't be moved from implicitly | `x`, `*p`, `arr[i]`, `std::cout`, a function returning `T&`, **a named rvalue reference** |
| **prvalue** (pure rvalue) | a temporary value with no identity | `42`, `x + 1`, `String("abc")`, a function returning `T` by value |
| **xvalue** (expiring) | has identity but is marked as movable | `std::move(x)`, a function returning `T&&`, `std::move(obj).member` |

glvalue = lvalue + xvalue; rvalue = prvalue + xvalue. Rule of thumb: **if it has a name, it's an lvalue**, even if its type is `T&&`.

Binding rules:

| | lvalue | rvalue |
|---|---|---|
| `T&` | yes | **no** |
| `const T&` | yes | yes (extends a temporary's lifetime) |
| `T&&` | **no** | yes |

```cpp
void f(String& s);        // (1)
void f(const String& s);  // (2)
void f(String&& s);       // (3)
String a("x");
f(a);             // (1)
f(String("y"));   // (3): prvalue prefers && over const&
f(std::move(a));  // (3)
String&& r = String("z");
f(r);             // (1)! r has a name, so it's an lvalue
```

notes.heading: std::move: just a cast
notes.body:
`std::move` doesn't move anything. It's an unconditional cast to an rvalue reference, which makes overload resolution pick the move constructor/assignment:

```cpp
template <typename T>
constexpr std::remove_reference_t<T>&& move(T&& t) noexcept {
    return static_cast<std::remove_reference_t<T>&&>(t);
}
```

The **move constructor** does the actual work (steals pointers). After a move, the source is in a **valid but unspecified state**: you may destroy it or assign to it; don't read its value. (Standard types leave a moved-from `std::string`/`std::vector` empty in practice; `std::unique_ptr` is guaranteed null.)

Traps:
- `std::move` on a **const** object yields `const T&&`, which binds to the **copy** constructor `T(const T&)`, so it silently copies.
- `std::move` of an `int` or a trivially copyable struct is a plain copy; moving only helps when there's a resource (heap buffer, file descriptor) to steal.
- Using a moved-from object (`std::move(v); v.size()` is fine only because `vector` defines it; logic that expects the old contents is a bug).

notes.heading: Universal (forwarding) references and reference collapsing
notes.body:
`T&&` is a **forwarding (universal) reference** only when `T` is being **deduced** at that point: `template<class T> void f(T&& x)` or `auto&& x = …`. It binds to anything and remembers whether the argument was an lvalue or rvalue in `T`.

Not forwarding references (just rvalue references):
- `void f(String&& s)` (no deduction)
- `template<class T> void f(std::vector<T>&& v)` (the form is `vector<T>&&`, not `T&&`)
- `template<class T> void f(const T&& x)` (const kills it)
- inside `template<class T> class Box { void put(T&& x); }`: `T` is already fixed by the class

**Reference collapsing** (only the compiler can form references to references, during deduction/typedefs):

| Combination | Result |
|---|---|
| `T& &` | `T&` |
| `T& &&` | `T&` |
| `T&& &` | `T&` |
| `T&& &&` | `T&&` |

Any lvalue reference wins. So with `f(x)` (lvalue): `T = int&`, param `int& && = int&`. With `f(5)`: `T = int`, param `int&&`.

notes.heading: std::forward and perfect forwarding
Real example: our own std::vector<> and why moves matter
notes.body:
**In class (Lec-9 `main.cpp`):** a templated `vector<T>` with `mSize`, `mCapacity` (starts at 4) and `T* mData`, plus:
- a copy constructor that prints "COPY CONSTRUCTOR VERY COSTLY" and allocates and copies every element (**deep copy**, O(n));
- a move constructor that prints "SHALLOW COPY CONSTRUCTION VERY CHEAP", takes `other.mData`, `mSize`, `mCapacity` and sets `other` to `nullptr`/0 (**O(1)**, three loads and stores, no allocation);
- `makeVector()` returning a local by value, and `func(T&& temp)` that builds `vector<int> b(std::forward<T>(temp));`, so it picks copy or move depending on the caller.

What it prints: in C++17 at default settings, `vector<int> a(makeVector());` prints three "PUSH" lines and `3` with **no** copy/move message (NRVO in `makeVector`, guaranteed elision for the prvalue). With `-fno-elide-constructors` the cheap move constructor shows up (once in C++17, twice in C++14).

Bugs in the class sketch worth spotting in an exam:

| Bug | Fix |
|---|---|
| Copy ctor takes `const vector<int>&` inside `vector<T>` | `const vector& other` (or `vector<T>`) |
| Copy loop runs `for (i < mSize)` **before** setting `mSize`, so it copies nothing (`mSize` is 0) | assign `mSize = other.mSize` first, or loop to `other.mSize` |
| No destructor: `mData` leaks | `~vector() { delete[] mData; }` |
| No copy/move assignment: defaults would do a shallow pointer copy, which is a double `delete[]` once a destructor exists | Rule of 5 (or copy-and-swap) |
| `pop_back` calls `mData[mSize].~T()` (one past the last element), and an explicit `~T()` on an element of `new T[]` is destroyed again by `delete[]` | `--mSize; mData[mSize].~T();` with raw storage plus placement new (that's what `std::vector` does) |
| `throw;` with no active exception calls `std::terminate` | throw a real exception or assert |
| `push_back` when full just returns | allocate 2x, **move** elements over, free the old buffer |
| Move constructor isn't `noexcept` | mark it `noexcept` (see below) |

**Why `noexcept` on the move constructor is a performance feature:** on reallocation, `std::vector` must keep the strong exception guarantee, so it uses `std::move_if_noexcept`: it moves elements only if the move constructor is `noexcept` (or the type can't be copied), otherwise it **copies** every element. A `vector<Order>` whose `Order(Order&&)` lacks `noexcept` deep-copies on every growth.

notes.heading: Rule of 0, 3 and 5 (a std::string-like class)
SSO: small string optimisation
notes.body:
A `std::string` is not just a pointer: it keeps a small **inline buffer** inside the object so that short strings (symbols like "AAPL", order IDs) need **no heap allocation**.

| Library | `sizeof(std::string)` | Inline capacity |
|---|---|---|
| libstdc++ (GCC, Linux) | 32 bytes | 15 chars |
| libc++ (Clang, macOS) | 24 bytes | 22 chars |
| MSVC | 32 bytes | 15 chars |

libstdc++ layout: `char* ptr; size_t size; union { size_t capacity; char buf[16]; }`, where `ptr` points into `buf` for short strings.

Consequences:
- Creating and copying short strings is cheap: no `new`, data on the same cache line as the object.
- **Moving an SSO string is not cheaper than copying it**: the bytes must be copied (there's no pointer to steal), and the source is reset. Moves only win for long (heap) strings.
- Crossing the threshold (16th char on libstdc++) triggers an allocation: a latency spike on the hot path.
- `std::string_view` (pointer + length, 16 bytes) avoids copies entirely for read-only parameters.
- HFT code often uses fixed-size `char sym[8]` or a `uint64_t`-packed symbol to make comparisons a single integer compare.

notes.heading: SFINAE
Concepts (C++20)
Type traits by template specialisation: is_move_constructible, is_destructible
RVO and NRVO
notes.body:
**RVO (Return Value Optimisation):** returning a **prvalue** (`return String("x");`). Since **C++17 this is guaranteed** ("mandatory copy elision"): the object is constructed directly in the caller's storage (the hidden return-slot pointer in `rdi`). No copy or move constructor is called, and the type doesn't even need one.

**NRVO (Named RVO):** returning a **named local** (`File a; … return a;`). It's **allowed but not guaranteed**; GCC/Clang do it whenever there's a single object returned on all paths. If it doesn't happen, the return is an **implicit move** (since C++11 a returned local is treated as an rvalue first), so you still don't copy.

**In class (Lec-9 `second.cpp`):** the instructor contrasted `return File({47674}, "...")` (RVO, an unnamed temporary) with `File a; /* use */ return a;` (NRVO) and `File a = construct();` in `main`.

When NRVO fails:

```cpp
S pick(bool b) { S a, c; if (b) return a; return c; }  // two named candidates -> move
S fromParam(S p) { return p; }                         // parameters are never elided -> implicit move
S fromMember()   { return this->member; }              // a member: COPY (not a local)
S bad() { S s; return std::move(s); }                  // pessimisation: blocks NRVO, forces a move
```

Rules for exams:
1. **Never write `return std::move(local);`** (GCC/Clang warn with `-Wpessimizing-move`).
2. Prefer one named result variable or returning prvalues.
3. Check with `-fno-elide-constructors` to see where copies/moves would happen, and on Compiler Explorer look for calls to `String(String&&)`.

notes.heading: Healthy C++ tricks: loving the compiler more
unique_ptr and shared_ptr (first look; the control block)
notes.body:
- `std::unique_ptr<T>`: **sole ownership**, move-only (copy is deleted), `sizeof` = one raw pointer (8 bytes) with the default deleter, and `->` costs the same as a raw pointer. It's what you hand out from factories: `auto o = std::make_unique<Order>(id, px, qty);`.
- `std::shared_ptr<T>`: **shared ownership** with reference counting. `sizeof` = **16 bytes** (pointer to the object plus a pointer to the **control block**).

The **control block** is a separate heap object holding:
1. the **strong count** (number of `shared_ptr` owners; when it hits 0 the object is destroyed),
2. the **weak count** (number of `weak_ptr`s, +1 while any strong owner exists; when it hits 0 the block itself is freed),
3. the **deleter** and allocator (type-erased),
4. with `make_shared`, the object itself is stored in the same allocation.

Copying a `shared_ptr` does an **atomic increment** (`lock xadd`), and destroying one does an atomic decrement: roughly 5–20 ns uncontended, far more when threads bounce the counter's cache line. `make_shared<T>(…)` does **one** allocation instead of two (object + control block) and keeps them adjacent in cache. Session 7 builds both from scratch.

notes.heading: Quick revision
notes.body:
- lvalue = has a name/identity; prvalue = pure temporary; xvalue = `std::move(x)`. A named `T&&` is an lvalue.
- `T&` binds lvalues, `const T&` binds both, `T&&` binds rvalues.
- `std::move` = `static_cast<remove_reference_t<T>&&>`; the move constructor does the stealing.
- Moved-from objects are valid but unspecified: destroy or reassign them.
- `std::move` on a const object copies.
- `T&&` is a forwarding reference only when `T` is deduced right there (also `auto&&`).
- Reference collapsing: any `&` wins; only `&& &&` gives `&&`.
- `std::forward<T>(x)`: conditional cast that restores the caller's value category; use it once per forwarding reference.
- Rule of 3/5: a resource-owning class needs destructor, copy ctor/assign, move ctor/assign; Rule of 0 is better.
- Declaring a destructor or copy op suppresses the implicit move ops.
- Copy-and-swap: `T& operator=(T other) noexcept { swap(other); return *this; }`.
- SSO: libstdc++ string is 32 B with 15 inline chars; libc++ is 24 B with 22; moving a short string still copies bytes.
- SFINAE: substitution failure in the signature removes the overload; errors in the body are hard errors.
- Concepts: `template<std::integral T>`, `requires` expressions, better errors, subsumption.
- `is_move_constructible<T>` = `is_constructible<T, T&&>`: true for copy-only types.
- `vector` moves on growth only if the move ctor is `noexcept` (move_if_noexcept).
- C++17: returning a prvalue is guaranteed elision; NRVO is optional; never `return std::move(local)`.
- `shared_ptr` = 16 B + a control block (strong count, weak count, deleter); copies are atomic increments.

notes.heading: Exam traps
notes.body:
- `void f(Order&& o) { store(o); }` copies: `o` has a name, so it's an lvalue. Write `store(std::move(o))`.
- `template<class T> void f(std::vector<T>&& v)` is **not** a forwarding reference; it only binds rvalues.
- `const std::string s = "…"; v.push_back(std::move(s));` copies (const&& binds to the copy ctor).
- `return std::move(local);` is slower (it disables NRVO), not faster.
- A class with a user-declared destructor and no move ops: `std::move(obj)` silently **copies**.
- `std::forward` without the explicit template argument doesn't compile (non-deduced context by design).
- Calling `std::forward<T>(x)` twice on the same argument can move from it twice: a use-after-move bug.
- `is_move_constructible_v<T>` being true does **not** mean T has a move constructor.
- A moved-from `std::string` is *usually* empty, but only "valid but unspecified" is guaranteed; `unique_ptr` is guaranteed null.
- Member initialiser order follows **declaration order**, not the order in the initialiser list.
- `-fno-elide-constructors` doesn't disable C++17 *guaranteed* elision, only NRVO and pre-C++17 elisions; that's why the class listing (built without guaranteed elision) shows two moves while C++17 shows none.
- SSO: moving a short `std::string` is about as costly as copying it.
- `shared_ptr` copies are thread-safe for the **count**, not for the pointed-to object.

keyTerms.def: An expression with identity (usually a name) that can't be implicitly moved from.
A pure temporary value such as `42` or `String("x")`, with no identity.
An expiring value with identity, e.g. the result of `std::move(x)`.
`T&&` (non-deduced): binds only to rvalues; used to detect movable temporaries.
`T&&` with `T` deduced (or `auto&&`): binds to anything and records the category in `T`.
Rule that a reference to a reference collapses to `&` unless both are `&&`.
Unconditional cast to an rvalue reference; enables move overloads.
Conditional cast that restores an argument's original value category.
`T(T&&) noexcept`: builds an object by stealing another's resources.
A resource owner defines destructor, copy ctor, copy assignment, move ctor and move assignment.
Use self-managing members so no special member functions need to be written.
Assignment taking its parameter by value and swapping, giving strong exception safety.
Small string optimisation: short strings stored inside the string object, no heap allocation.
Substitution Failure Is Not An Error: overloads whose signature fails substitution are dropped.
C++20 named compile-time predicate constraining template parameters.
Produces a `T&&` in unevaluated contexts without constructing a T.
Constructing a returned prvalue directly in the caller's storage; guaranteed since C++17.
Eliding the copy/move of a returned named local; permitted but not guaranteed.
Casts to rvalue only if the move ctor is noexcept (or no copy exists); used by vector growth.
shared_ptr's heap bookkeeping: strong count, weak count, deleter, allocator (and object with make_shared).

mcqs.explanation: r has a name, so the expression `r` is an lvalue of type String, and the best match is the non-const lvalue reference.
mcqs.distractors: Its declared type is String&&, but value category depends on the expression, not on how the variable was declared.

mcqs.q: What does `std::move(x)` actually do at runtime?
options: Sets x to its default state
Nothing by itself: it's a cast to an rvalue reference
mcqs.explanation: std::move is just `static_cast<T&&>`; any moving is done by the move constructor or assignment that the cast lets overload resolution select.
mcqs.distractors: Constructors and resets happen only if the result is used to initialise or assign something.

mcqs.explanation: std::move on a const object gives `const S&&`, which can't bind to `S&&` but can bind to `const S&`, so the copy constructor runs.
mcqs.distractors: There's no compile error because the copy constructor is a valid fallback; elision doesn't apply to an existing named object.

mcqs.q: In which declaration is `T&&` a forwarding (universal) reference?
options: `template<class T> struct Box { void put(T&& x); };`
mcqs.explanation: Only the plain `T&&` form, with T deduced at that call, is a forwarding reference.
mcqs.distractors: vector<T>&& and const T&& are plain rvalue references, and in a class member T is already fixed by the class.

mcqs.q: With `template<class T> void f(T&& p);` and `int x;`, what is the type of `p` in `f(x)`?
mcqs.explanation: T is deduced as int&, and `int& &&` collapses to `int&`.
mcqs.distractors: int&& would be the result for an rvalue argument.

mcqs.q: In class we wrote `func(T&& obj) { utils::Forward<T>(obj).print(); }` with `print() const &` printing "L value" and `print() const &&` printing "R value". What does `const X a; func(a); func(X{});` print?
mcqs.explanation: For the lvalue a, T = const X&, so Forward returns an lvalue: L value. For the prvalue X{}, T = X and Forward returns X&&: R value.
mcqs.distractors: L value, L value is what you'd get by calling obj.print() directly, without forwarding.

mcqs.q: Why is `utils::Forward`'s parameter declared as `typename Remove_Ref<T>::type&` instead of `T&`?
options: To allow it to bind to rvalues only
Because references to references are illegal
To make T non-deduced, so callers must write Forward<T>(x) explicitly
mcqs.explanation: A nested `::type` is a non-deduced context; if T were deduced from the named argument it would always see an lvalue and forwarding would be lost.
mcqs.distractors: It has nothing to do with speed and still binds lvalues; collapsing rules make references to references fine during deduction.

mcqs.q: Which is the best signature for a constructor that **stores** a string member (an "Instrument" storing its symbol)?
mcqs.explanation: A by-value sink plus move costs one copy for an lvalue argument and zero copies (just moves) for an rvalue.
mcqs.distractors: A const by-value parameter can't be moved from; `sym(s)` with a named `&&` copies; a non-const `&` rejects temporaries.

mcqs.q: A `std::vector<Order>` reallocates. `Order` has a user-written move constructor **without** `noexcept`, and a copy constructor. What does vector do with the existing elements?
options: Leaves them in place and links a new block
mcqs.explanation: vector keeps the strong exception guarantee with move_if_noexcept: a throwing move could leave both buffers broken, so it copies when the move isn't noexcept and a copy exists.
mcqs.distractors: vector's storage must be contiguous, and memcpy is only used for trivially copyable types.

mcqs.q: Which class has **no** implicitly generated move constructor?
mcqs.explanation: A user-declared destructor suppresses the implicit move constructor and move assignment, so `std::move(c)` falls back to the copy constructor.
mcqs.distractors: Declaring a default constructor doesn't affect moves; A, B and D get implicit memberwise moves.

mcqs.q: On GCC/libstdc++ (x86-64 Linux), what are `sizeof(std::string)` and its SSO capacity?
mcqs.explanation: libstdc++ stores a pointer, a size and a 16-byte union (capacity or inline buffer): 32 bytes, with 15 chars plus the '\0' inline.
mcqs.distractors: 24/22 is libc++ (Clang/macOS); a string is never just a single pointer.

mcqs.q: Why is moving a 5-character `std::string` not meaningfully cheaper than copying it?
options: Because std::string has no move constructor
With SSO the characters live inside the object, so they have to be copied anyway; there's no heap pointer to steal
Because short strings are reference counted
mcqs.explanation: A move only beats a copy when there's an external buffer to transfer; inline SSO bytes must be copied.
mcqs.distractors: std::string does have a noexcept move ctor, and C++11 forbids copy-on-write strings.

mcqs.q: What does SFINAE stand for and where does it apply?
options: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error; anywhere in the function body
Static Function Inlining Not An Error; anywhere in the body
Substitution Failure Is Not An Error; only in the immediate context of the signature
Specialization First, Instantiation Next; only for class templates
mcqs.explanation: Failed substitution in the declaration (parameter types, return type, default template args) removes the overload; errors in the body are hard errors.
mcqs.distractors: The body is not part of the immediate context, so the 'anywhere in the body' options are wrong.

mcqs.q: Which is a correct C++20 constrained function template accepting only integral prices?
options: `template<class T> requires std::integral<T> T mid(T a, T b);`
`template<std::is_integral T> T mid(T a, T b);`
`template<class T> T mid(T a, T b) requires std::is_integral_v;`
mcqs.explanation: A requires-clause with the std::integral concept is valid (as is `template<std::integral T>`).
mcqs.distractors: std::is_integral is a trait class, not a concept; is_integral_v needs a template argument; `concept<int>` isn't syntax.

mcqs.q: `struct NoMove { NoMove(const NoMove&); };` (copy constructor declared, move not declared). What is `std::is_move_constructible_v<NoMove>`?
options: true: an rvalue can bind to `const NoMove&`
mcqs.explanation: The trait asks whether `NoMove(std::declval<NoMove&&>())` is well-formed; the copy constructor accepts it, so it's true. It would be false only if the move ctor were explicitly deleted.
mcqs.distractors: The trait tests constructibility from an rvalue, not the existence of a T(T&&) signature.

mcqs.q: Which `return` is a **guaranteed** elision in C++17?
mcqs.explanation: Returning a prvalue is mandatory copy elision in C++17: the object is constructed directly in the caller's storage.
mcqs.distractors: Returning a named local is optional NRVO; std::move blocks it; parameters are never elided (they're implicitly moved).

mcqs.q: Why is `return std::move(local);` a bad idea?
options: It disables NRVO and forces a move constructor call that would otherwise be elided
It doesn't compile for move-only types
mcqs.explanation: The expression is no longer just the name of a local, so NRVO can't apply; a plain `return local;` is either elided or implicitly moved anyway.
mcqs.distractors: It's legal and works for move-only types, it's just slower; it moves, not copies.

mcqs.q: In class, our custom String's objdump showed `concat()` calling `String(char const*)` then `String(String&&)`, and `main` calling `String(String&&)` again. Under default C++17 compilation, how many move-constructor calls does that program make?
mcqs.explanation: Both `return String("…")` and `String c{concat(a,b)}` initialise from prvalues, which C++17 guarantees to elide; the listing came from a build without guaranteed elision.
mcqs.distractors: 1 or 2 moves would only appear with -fno-elide-constructors and pre-C++17 rules.

mcqs.q: In class Lec-9 `vector`, the copy constructor runs `for (i = 0; i < mSize; ++i) mData[i] = other.mData[i];` and only then sets `mSize = other.mSize`. What's the effect?
options: Copies nothing: mSize is still 0 during the loop, so the new vector has the right size but uninitialised contents
mcqs.explanation: Default member initialisers set mSize to 0, so the loop body never runs; then mSize is set, leaving garbage elements.
mcqs.distractors: The loop bound is 0, so it can neither overrun nor loop forever.

mcqs.q: What is stored in a `std::shared_ptr`'s control block?
options: Only the pointer to the object
A mutex and the object copy
The strong count, weak count, deleter (and allocator); with make_shared, also the object
mcqs.explanation: The control block holds both reference counts and the type-erased deleter/allocator; make_shared co-locates the object with it in one allocation.
mcqs.distractors: Counts are atomics, not mutexes, and the object's vtable is unrelated.

mcqs.q: What is `sizeof(std::shared_ptr<int>)` on x86-64 with GCC or Clang?
mcqs.explanation: Two pointers: one to the managed object and one to the control block.
mcqs.distractors: 8 is unique_ptr with the default deleter; the counts live in the control block, not in the shared_ptr.

msqs.q: Which expressions are rvalues (prvalue or xvalue)? (select all that apply)
msqs.explanation: Literals and arithmetic results are prvalues, std::move(x) is an xvalue. A named rvalue reference is an lvalue, and dereferencing gives an lvalue.

msqs.q: Which are forwarding (universal) references? (select all that apply)
msqs.explanation: T&&, auto&& and a pack Ts&&... with deduction are forwarding references. A concrete Order&& and const T&& are plain rvalue references.

msqs.q: Which reference-collapsing results are correct? (select all that apply)
msqs.explanation: Any lvalue reference in the pair wins, so only && && collapses to &&; `int&& &` collapses to int&.

msqs.q: Which statements about std::move and std::forward are true? (select all that apply)
options: std::move is an unconditional cast to an rvalue reference
std::move on a const object usually ends up calling the copy constructor
std::forward<T>(x) casts to rvalue only when T is a non-reference type (caller passed an rvalue)
std::move frees the source object's memory
std::forward deduces T automatically from its argument
msqs.explanation: move always casts, forward casts conditionally, and const&& binds the copy ctor. forward's parameter is a non-deduced context so you must write the T, and move frees nothing.

msqs.q: A class owns a raw `char*` buffer from `new[]`. Which special members must it handle correctly to follow the Rule of 5? (select all that apply)
msqs.explanation: The Rule of 5 is destructor, copy ctor, copy assignment, move ctor and move assignment. The default constructor isn't part of it.

msqs.q: Which bugs were present in the class's custom String (Lec-8)? (select all that apply)
options: The move constructor used `other->mSize` on a reference
There was no copy assignment, so `a = b` would shallow-copy the pointer
It used a stack array instead of the heap
The copy constructor shared the source's pointer instead of allocating
The destructor never called `delete[]`, so the buffer leaked
msqs.explanation: The move ctor's `->` doesn't compile on a reference, the destructor just nulled the pointer, and the missing assignment operators mean a memberwise (shallow) copy. The copy ctor did allocate and deep-copy, and the buffer was on the heap.

msqs.q: Which bugs are in the class's Lec-9 vector sketch? (select all that apply)
options: `pop_back` destroys `mData[mSize]`, one past the last element
The move constructor deep-copies the elements
push_back when full returns silently instead of growing
`throw;` with no active exception calls std::terminate
msqs.explanation: All of those are real defects. The move constructor correctly steals the pointer and nulls the source: that part is right.

msqs.q: Which of these copy (rather than move or elide) the Order? (select all that apply)
options: `v.push_back(std::move(order));` where order is a non-const local
msqs.explanation: A named && parameter is an lvalue, std::move of a const object binds the copy ctor, and returning a member is a copy (members aren't implicitly moved). Moving a non-const local moves, and returning a prvalue is guaranteed elision.

msqs.q: Which statements about SSO (small string optimisation) are true? (select all that apply)

short.q: Explain the difference between `std::move` and `std::forward`, and when you use each. Include how `std::forward` is implemented.

checks.label: move is an unconditional cast to rvalue
forward is conditional, preserving the value category
forward is used with forwarding/universal references

short.modelAnswer:
`std::move(x)` is an **unconditional** cast to an rvalue reference (`static_cast<std::remove_reference_t<T>&&>(x)`). Use it on an object you own and won't use again, to let a move constructor/assignment steal its resources.

`std::forward<T>(x)` is a **conditional** cast: it returns an rvalue only if the original argument was an rvalue (T deduced as a non-reference type), so it **preserves the original value category**. Use it only inside a template on a **forwarding reference** `T&&` to pass the argument on unchanged (perfect forwarding: `emplace_back`, `make_unique`, wrappers).

```cpp
template <class T>
T&& forward(std::remove_reference_t<T>& x) noexcept { return static_cast<T&&>(x); }
```

If T = `X&`, `T&&` collapses to `X&` (lvalue stays lvalue); if T = `X`, it's `X&&`. The parameter type is a **non-deduced** context, so you must write `std::forward<T>(x)` with the explicit template argument. That's exactly the `utils::Forward` we wrote in class on top of our `Remove_Ref` trait.
short.explanation: Expect: unconditional vs conditional, forwarding references, static_cast<T&&> with collapsing, and the explicit T.

short.q: What are RVO and NRVO? Which one is guaranteed in C++17, and why should you not write `return std::move(local);`?

checks.label: RVO is for returning a prvalue / temporary
NRVO is for a named local
RVO is guaranteed since C++17, NRVO isn't
Object constructed directly in the caller's storage

short.modelAnswer:
**RVO** (return value optimisation) applies when you return a **prvalue/temporary**: `return File(fd, path);`. Since **C++17 it's guaranteed** (mandatory copy elision): the object is constructed directly in the **caller's** storage via the hidden return-slot pointer, with no copy or move constructor at all.

**NRVO** applies to a **named** local: `File a; …; return a;`. It's permitted but **not guaranteed**; compilers do it when one object is returned on every path. If they can't, the returned local is **implicitly moved**, never copied.

`return std::move(local);` turns the operand into an xvalue expression, which **blocks NRVO** and forces a move constructor call that would otherwise have been elided: a pessimisation (`-Wpessimizing-move`). Just write `return local;`.
short.explanation: Distinguish prvalue (guaranteed) vs named (optional), say where the object is built, and say why std::move hurts.

checks.label: Copy loop uses mSize before it's set (copies nothing)
Parameter should be vector<T> / vector, not vector<int>

short.modelAnswer:
1. The copy constructor takes `const vector<int>&`; inside `vector<T>` it should be `const vector& other` (`vector<T>`), otherwise it isn't a copy constructor for `vector<double>`.
2. The loop runs `i < mSize` while `mSize` is still **0** (default member initialiser), so it **copies nothing**; the elements are left default-initialised. Loop to `other.mSize` or set `mSize` first.
3. There's **no destructor**, so `mData` **leaks**; and once one is added, the implicit copy/move assignment would shallow-copy `mData` and double `delete[]`. Apply the Rule of 5.
4. `pop_back` is **off by one**: `mData[mSize]` is one past the last element. It should be `--mSize; mData[mSize].~T();`. Even then, calling `~T()` on an element created by `new T[]` means `delete[]` destroys it again; a real vector uses raw storage plus placement new.
5. A bare `throw;` with no active exception calls `std::terminate`; throw `std::out_of_range` or assert.
6. Not shown, but the move constructor should be `noexcept`, and `push_back` must grow (2x) instead of returning.
short.explanation: Spot the uninitialised-size loop, the wrong parameter type, the leak, the off-by-one and the bare throw.

short.q: Explain SSO in std::string: give sizes for libstdc++ and libc++, and say why it matters for low-latency code.

checks.label: Short strings stored inline in the object, no heap
Avoids allocation / latency spike when it grows
Moving a short string still copies the bytes

short.modelAnswer:
SSO (small string optimisation) keeps short strings **inline**, inside the string object itself, so no heap allocation happens. libstdc++ (GCC): `sizeof(std::string)` = **32** bytes with a 16-byte buffer, so up to **15** chars plus `'\0'`. libc++ (Clang): **24** bytes, up to **22** chars.

Why it matters: most symbols, venue codes and short IDs fit, so creating and copying them doesn't call `malloc` (which costs tens of ns to microseconds and can contend), and the data sits on the same cache line as the object. But a string that grows past the inline capacity suddenly **allocates**, a latency spike on the hot path. Also, **moving** a short string isn't cheaper than copying: there's no heap pointer to steal, so the inline bytes are copied. HFT code often uses fixed `char[8]` or integer-packed symbols to make comparisons a single instruction.
short.explanation: They want the inline-buffer idea, the correct sizes, the allocation/latency point and the move-isn't-free caveat.
